question_en: When inventory costs are declining, a company using FIFO will most likely experience:
explanation_en:
FIFO (first-in, first-out) inventory costing means that a company is deemed to have sold its older inventory first. When inventory costs fall, older
inventory is valued higher than more recently purchased inventory. The older inventory is included in the cost of goods sold (COGS), so a higher-
valued inventory equals higher COGS. Gross profit is the difference between revenues and COGS, so a higher COGS translates to lower profits.
When older inventory is sold first, ending inventory consists of the more recent purchases. With falling inventory costs, more recent purchases are
less costly than the older ones, so ending inventory is worth less than beginning inventory. Inventory is a current asset, and the current ratio is
calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities. A lower ending inventory value means a lower value for both current assets and the
current ratio.
(Choice B) Since COGS is higher when inventory costs fall (using FIFO), gross profit is lower, not higher. The gross profit margin is equal to
gross profit divided by revenues, so the gross profit margin is also less.
(Choice C) Working capital is the difference between current assets and current liabilities. A lower inventory value results in lower working
capital.

question_en:
An engineering company manufactures high-end automotive accessories. It reports under US GAAP and uses LIFO. The company is replacing its inventory for the coming year and has determined that its existing inventory has become obsolete. An analyst gathers the following Information:

| Per-Unit Inventory | USD |
|---|---|
| Original cost | 105 |
| Selling price | 150 |
| Replacement cost | 96 |
| Net realizable value | 100 |
| Normal profit margin | 7 |

The per-unit value that the company reports for the existing inventory is closest to:
explanation_en:
US GAAP require companies using LIFO to report inventory at the lower of historic cost or market value. US GAAP define market value as
replacement cost (subject to upper and lower limits). The upper limit is net realizable value, which equals the selling price minus costs to
complete and sell the inventory. The lower limit is net realizable value minus a normal profit margin.
When the replacement cost falls between the two limits, as is the case here, then it is used as the market value, which is then compared to the
historic cost. The diagram below illustrates this concept:
(Choice B) $100 represents the upper bound for market value. This would be the correct answer if the replacement cost were higher than the
inventory's net realizable value.

question_en: A company that reports under IFRS is valuing its year-end inventory. It has collected the following information (in CHF millions): Based on this data, the inventory value (in CHF millions) reported on its balance sheet is closest to:
explanation_en:
Inventory is initially recorded on a company's balance sheet at historic cost. However, companies are required to regularly reassess this value. If
the inventory's value falls below its cost (eg, spoils, becomes obsolete, declines in selling price), the company must write down the inventory to
reflect the new, lower value, which becomes the carrying value.
IFRS require companies to report the carrying value of inventory at the lower of cost or net realizable value (NRV). The NRV is the estimated
selling price less the cost of completing and selling the inventory.
In this scenario, the NRV of the inventory is CHF 180 million (240 − 60). This is higher than the cost of 175, so no write down is taken and the
inventory remains at 175.
(Choice A) 165 is the replacement value, which is not used by IFRS in valuing inventory. The replacement value is used by companies reporting
under US GAAP and using LIFO or retail inventory methods when valuing inventory.
(Choice C) 180 is the NRV, which is greater than the historical cost. Since inventory is required to be valued at the lower of cost and NRV, the
company would not be permitted to increase the value of its inventory above 175.

question_en: Which of the following types of ratio will most likely be positively affected by an inventory write-down?
explanation_en:
Companies write down the carrying value of inventory on the books due to spoilage, obsolescence, or reductions in selling prices. When a
write-down occurs, the company decreases inventory on the balance sheet and increases COGS on the income statement, both by the amount of
the write-down. These adjustments have a negative impact on liquidity and profitability ratios and an artificially positive impact on activity ratios.
Activity ratios measure efficiency. One common example is inventory turnover (or COGS / Inventory), which measures the average number of
times a company sells its average inventory over a period. After a write-down, the ratio becomes higher since an inventory write-down increases
COGS (numerator) and decreases inventory (denominator). This makes a company appear to be more efficient at turning its inventory into sales.
Analysts should be aware of the impact of such practices and make appropriate adjustments when analyzing financial reports.
(Choice B) Liquidity ratios measure a company's ability to cover short-term obligations. They commonly consist of current assets (including
inventory) in the numerator and current liabilities in the denominator. Decreasing inventory value reduces the numerator, which worsens the ratio.
(Choice C) Profitability ratios measure a type of profit as a fraction of revenue. Write-downs increase COGS, an expense, thereby decreasing all
types of profitability.

question_en: A manufacturing company that uses LIFO under US GAAP shows the following inventory-related information at the end of 20X8: Based on this data, the inventory amount reported on the balance sheet (in $ millions) is closest to:
explanation_en:
Inventory may lose value due to spoilage, obsolescence, or declines in selling prices. Companies often update their inventory values on the
balance sheet to account for such events. US GAAP require companies using LIFO to report inventory at the lower of historic cost or market
value (MV).
MV is defined as the current replacement cost (RC) subject to an upper and lower limit.
The upper limit is the net realizable value (NRV), which equals the selling price minus costs to complete and sell the inventory. In this
scenario, the upper limit (NRV) equals the selling price (110) minus the completion cost (15), or 95.
The lower limit is the NRV minus a normal profit margin. In this scenario, the lower limit equals NRV (95) minus a normal profit margin (20),
or 75.
The MV is 75 since the RC of 70 is subject to a lower limit of 75 (ie, cannot fall below 75). Since the company must record inventory at the lower
of cost or market, it must update its inventory amount on the balance sheet to 75.
Note: MV is always the middle number of the RC, upper limit, and lower limit, when ranked in order:
If RC > Upper > Lower, MV is the upper limit.
If Upper > RC > Lower, MV is the RC.
If Upper > Lower > RC, MV is the lower limit.
(Choice A) 70 results from not imposing a lower limit of 75 on the RC.
(Choice C) 95 is the NRV, which is the upper limit.

question_en: Unlike companies that comply with US GAAP, a company reporting under IFRS can disclose in its financial statements the amount of:
option_c: a reversal of an inventory write-down.
explanation_en:
Inventory constitutes a large percentage of total assets for many companies and can significantly impact revenue, expenses (ie, cost of sales),
and liquidity. As such, companies provide inventory-related disclosures in financial statements to better explain reporting methods and trends.
One important category of disclosure relates to reversals of previously written down inventory, which is permitted under IFRS only. In general,
a write-down occurs when an inventory item's market value falls below its carrying value on the balance sheet. A write-down increases expenses
(cost of sales) and lowers profits. Any subsequent reversals of write-downs will allow companies to recapture these lost profits.
(Choice A) LIFO reporting is allowed under US GAAP, not IFRS. LIFO reserves measure the difference between ending inventory value
measured under FIFO and LIFO and are reported only for US GAAP companies.
(Choice B) Companies using both US GAAP and IFRS disclose information related to inventory write-downs.

question_en: A company reporting under US GAAP has both increasing inventory levels and increasing inventory unit costs. Which inventory valuation method most likely results in the lowest days of inventory on hand?
explanation_en:
Rising and falling inventory unit costs will have different effects on a company's reported financials depending on its inventory valuation method.
With the LIFO method, during periods of rising costs and steady-to-increasing inventory quantities, the most expensive inventory is included in a
company's COGS, resulting in a higher COGS when compared to other inventory methods. In addition, ending inventory is lower since the least
expensive units remain in inventory.
A company's days of inventory on hand is equal to 365 days in a year divided by the company's inventory turnover ratio. The more frequently a
company turns over its inventory, the fewer days it remains on hand.
Since a company using LIFO has a higher COGS and lower inventory, its inventory turnover is higher. Days of inventory are inversely affected
since inventory turnover is the denominator. Therefore, days of inventory on hand are lower for a company using LIFO compared to a company
using FIFO during a period of rising inventory costs (Choice B).
(Choice C) Using the weighted average cost method results in an amount of COGS between LIFO and FIFO. Therefore, using this method, days
of inventory on hand are not the lowest of the given methods.

question_en: Which of the following statements best describes the revaluation model and cost model for valuing long-lived tangible assets?
option_a: Both models compare historical costs to fair value.
option_b: Only the revaluation model uses the lower of historical cost or fair value.
option_c: Under the cost model, carrying values are always less than or equal to historical costs.
explanation_en: Long-lived asset valuations Revaluation model Cost model Beginning carrying value Historical cost Depreciation for all years Accumulated depreciation Fair value adjustment Revaluation = Not applicable Current fair value − carrying value Ending carrying value Historical cost Historical cost −Accumulated depreciation −Accumulated depreciation ± Revaluation IFRS, but not US GAAP, allow companies to choose between the cost model or the revaluation model for valuing long-lived assets. Using the cost model, an asset's carrying value is its historical cost less accumulated depreciation. The cost model only allows decreases in the carrying value of a long-lived asset, which could result from depreciation or impairment. Therefore, the cost model always reports an asset's carrying value below its historical cost. Using the revaluation model, the asset's carrying value changes based on its fair value. Revaluations adjust an asset's carrying value upward or downward. An initial upward revaluation suggests that a company reports the asset on the balance sheet at a higher value than its original cost. explanation_en: Treatment for intangible assets Acquisition method Treatment of costs Purchased on a stand-alone basis Fair value of assets capitalized on balance sheet Research costs expensed immediately on income statement Developed internally through research Development costs capitalized on balance sheet if product is developed for internal use (US and development GAAP) or has demonstrated technical feasibility (IFRS) Acquired through a business Fair value of assets capitalized on balance sheet combination (eg, merger) Additional goodwill created on balance sheet Long-lived assets that lack physical substance and are nonfinancial in nature are called intangible assets. question_en: A company capitalized a ¥120 million equipment purchase at the beginning of this year and will use straight-line depreciation with zero salvage value and a three-year useful life. The company generates ¥200 million in revenue every year, and the tax rate is 25%. If depreciation and taxes are the only expenses, and based only on this information, the second year's ending financial results most likely show:
explanation_en: Impairment typically arises from an unanticipated decline in an asset's value. An asset is impaired when its carrying amount (ie, its book value) is greater than its recoverable amount. Under US GAAP, the recoverable amount is measured as the sum of the asset's undiscounted future cash flows, which represents total future economic benefits. Simply stated, an asset is impaired if its expected future benefits are below its current book value. When impairment occurs, the value of the asset is reduced on the balance sheet and an impairment charge is simultaneously reported on the income statement. According to US GAAP, impairment charges may never be reversed, even if the asset's value increases in the future. (Choices A and B) Under US GAAP, impairment occurs when the carrying value is more than the sum of the undiscounted future cash flows.

question_en:
An analyst has collected the following information on a technology company that reports financial results using US GAAP:

| 20X7 | $ thousands |
|---|---|
| Gross profit | 25,000 |
| Research and development expenses | (5,000) |
| Depreciation and amortization expenses | (4,000) |
| Total equity (beginning of year) | 100,000 |
| Total equity (end of year) | 120,000 |
| Tax rate | 25% |

The company amortizes intangible assets over a five-year period using straight-line depreciation. Assume that the company can elect to either expense or capitalize its research and development costs. If it had capitalized all research and development costs in 20X7, its return on equity for 20X7 would be closest to:
explanation_en:
Capitalizing R&D removes the $5,000 thousand R&D expense from the income statement but adds $5,000 thousand to noncurrent intangible assets, amortized straight-line over 5 years, which adds $1,000 thousand of amortization expense in 20X7.

Expensed: EBITDA 20,000; less D&A 4,000; EBT 16,000; less tax at 25% (4,000); net income 12,000.
Capitalized: EBITDA 25,000 (R&D no longer expensed); less D&A 5,000 (4,000 + 1,000 additional amortization); EBT 20,000; less tax at 25% (5,000); net income 15,000.

Capitalizing increases net income by 15,000 - 12,000 = 3,000, which also increases ending equity by the same after-tax amount: ending equity = 120,000 + 3,000 = 123,000 (beginning equity is unchanged at 100,000, since this is the first year the R&D would have been capitalized).

ROE = Net income / Average equity = 15,000 / [(100,000 + 123,000) / 2] = 15,000 / 111,500 ≈ 13.4%.

An impairment loss under IFRS equals the difference between the carrying amount and the recoverable amount. Here is an example of the impairment loss calculation under IFRS, using the appropriate recoverable amount: In this example, the company reduces the asset by EUR 15,000 on the balance sheet and simultaneously records an impairment loss of EUR 15,000 on the income statement. IFRS, but not US GAAP, permit companies to revalue noncurrent assets to reflect their fair value. Revaluations can be up or down, and impact
both the income statement and the balance sheet. An upward revaluation means that the company reports the asset on the balance sheet at a
higher value than its original cost. This increase in the asset's carrying value results in a corresponding increase in shareholders' equity.
For initial upward revaluations, the increase in value bypasses the income statement and is reported in other comprehensive income (OCI);
it has no impact on net income. Both return on assets (ROA) and return on equity (ROE) use net income as the numerator. Neither ratio's
numerator changes, so both will be lower, not higher (Choice C).
The leverage ratio is calculated as average total assets divided by average shareholders' equity. Unless a company has zero liabilities,
average assets is always greater than average equity. When a ratio is greater than one, adding the same amount to both the numerator and
denominator causes that ratio to decrease, not increase (Choice B).

question_en: A company purchases a piece of capital equipment at the beginning of the year. The equipment has a useful life of three years and zero salvage value. All else being equal, compared to capitalizing the expenditure, if the company expenses the purchase, it would most appropriately report:
option_a: lower total cash after three years.
option_b: the same cumulative net income over three years.
option_c: lower cash flow from investing over the three years.
explanation_en:
Expensing an asset purchase initially reports the amount of the expenditure on the income statement whereas capitalizing an asset
purchase initially reports the amount of the expenditure on the balance sheet. Each method initially impacts the company's financial results
differently, but the cumulative impact to net income and total cash flow under both methods is the same over time.
The example below shows this application for a ¥90 million asset purchase. This example assumes straight-line depreciation but would be true of
any depreciation method:
If the company expenses the asset, the cost of ¥90 million is recorded one time on the income statement that year. As a result, net income and
operating cash flow are initially low but subsequently recover in future years.
If the company capitalizes the asset, the cost of ¥90 million is instead reported on the balance sheet as a long-term asset upon initial recognition
and subsequently spread to the income statement as a depreciation expense over the asset's useful life (ie, ¥30 million annually). Therefore, the
impact to net income and operating cash flow is reflected each year. However, at the end of three years, the cumulative impact to net income and
total cash flow is the same.

pdf: D:\CLAUDE\Projet CFA\CFA L1\6. TOUGH QB UWORLD-2000 MCQs\5. Financial Statement Analysis\5.07 Analysis of Long-Term Assets - Answers.pdf
question_en: A company has equipment with a carrying value of USD 2 million. If the company reclassifies the equipment as held for use until disposal, the company most likely:
option_a: continues to report depreciation and impairment charges.
option_b: no longer reports impairment charges but continues reporting depreciation.
option_c: no longer reports depreciation but continues reporting impairment charges.
explanation_en:
A company may dispose of an asset by selling, exchanging, distributing, or abandoning it. If a noncurrent asset is considered held for sale (ie,
will be sold), the company no longer records depreciation expense or impairment charges.
If the asset is to be abandoned, exchanged, or distributed, it is classified as held for use until disposal. In this scenario, management will
continue to report depreciation expenses and test the asset for impairment since the asset's carrying value is greater than zero (USD 2
million). This lasts from the initial classification until the asset's disposal or until management reclassifies the asset (Choices B and C).
